phrase: deep Tube reconditioning works (which include PV conversion to Delkor)
problem: The words in brackets are not in the Head of Track's 9 Dec 2022 letter. Its answer 5 only lists sites under a heading and says nothing about Pandrol Vanguard (PV) or Delkor for any of them. The bracket comes from a different document by a different author 20 months later: Claire Mann, Chief Operating Officer, 9 Aug 2024. That letter says PV conversion to Delkor was done 'as part of Deep Tube Reconditioning at seven locations' but does not name them. It does not say that all reconditioning works include PV conversion, or that the Liverpool Street to Bethnal Green eastbound track has PV. The same letter also lists other PV approaches, such as PV removed and rails replaced at two sites. Because the bracket sits inside what the Head of Track 'reported', it puts words in his mouth. It also implies, with no source, that PV is fitted on the eastbound Liverpool Street to Bethnal Green track. The project's own claims ledger (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md, Reconditioning row) says we cannot say 'that it was done, or that Pandrol Vanguard is present'. The error carries into ASK-2 ('Deep Tube Reconditioning works (replacing Pandrol Vanguard with Delkor)'), which would put a premise to TfL that no source supports. The TfL panel slide of 6 Dec 2022 (CSOPP p.11) does describe reconditioning in general as 'to replace Pandrol Vanguard with Delkor', but C03 does not cite it, and it says nothing about this site.
source_evidence: Weir-letter-2022-12#001 (Duncan Weir, Head of Track, to Zack Polanski AM, Chair, Environment Committee): '5. Provide a list of the deep Tube reconditioning sites ... Deep Tube reconditioning works planned for financial year 2023/24 ... Liverpool Street - Bethnal Green Eastbound Central'. The letter has no PV or Delkor wording for these sites. TfL-noise-update-2024-08#000 (Claire Mann, Chief Operating Officer, 9 August 2024): 'We have completed PV conversion to Delkor as part of Deep Tube Reconditioning at seven locations' and 'We have removed PV and replaced rails at two sites'. No locations are named. No chunk in the corpus links Pandrol Vanguard or Delkor to Liverpool Street-Bethnal Green.
suggested_wording: In a letter of 09 December 2022 to the Chair of the London Assembly Environment Committee, TfL's Head of Track listed 'Liverpool Street - Bethnal Green Eastbound Central' among 'Deep Tube reconditioning works planned for financial year 2023/24'. The letter does not say what the works at this site involve. None of the sources reviewed says whether Pandrol Vanguard is fitted there or whether the works were carried out. (Remove the TfL-noise-update-2024-08 citation from this claim, and delete '(replacing Pandrol Vanguard with Delkor)' from ASK-2.)

phrase: stated that it would undertake rail grinding at that location in February 2019
problem: 'That location' reads as the 720-880 m stretch named just before it. In the FOI, though, the grinding sentence answers a different question (when work will be done) and comes before the roughness finding, which answers the monitoring question. TfL's 'this location' means the Bethnal Green to Mile End stretch the requester asked about, not a grind aimed at 720-880 m. The claim also drops TfL's stated purpose and caveats. These matter because C02 follows C01 in a section about grinding for noise. TfL said: the grinding was 'with the intention to improve the wheel-rail interface'; a noise reduction 'is not guaranteed'; rail grinding 'is not deemed as an engineering method to reduce noise'; and Bethnal Green to Mile End is a location where further noise reduction is 'not technically practicable'. Without these, a reader may take it as a TfL promise to grind the rough stretch for noise. The claim does correctly present the grinding as an intention, not as done.
source_evidence: FOI-1730-1819#000: 'Whilst rail grinding is not deemed as an engineering method to reduce noise, some residents have experienced a reduction in noise levels following grinding. Rail grinding is primarily undertaken to reduce the growth rate of cracks and to improve the wheel-rail interface which can cause noise. We will undertake rail grinding at this location in February 2019, with the intention to improve the wheel-rail interface. There may be a reduction in noise level however this is not guaranteed.' Earlier in the same answer: 'This is one of the locations where current technology and the age of the track mean that it is not technically practicable to reduce the noise and vibration any further.' The 720-880m sentence comes later, under the monitoring question.
suggested_wording: In FOI-1730-1819 (published 22 October 2018), TfL said it would 'undertake rail grinding at this location in February 2019, with the intention to improve the wheel-rail interface', referring to the Central line between Bethnal Green and Mile End. It added that 'There may be a reduction in noise level however this is not guaranteed' and that rail grinding 'is not deemed as an engineering method to reduce noise'.

phrase: elevated rail roughness between 720 and 880m on the Central line between Bethnal Green and Mile End
problem: The roughness plots TfL attached cover the eastbound track only. They are dated January 2018, nine months before the FOI reply. The claim's wording suggests the whole section, possibly both tracks, and gives no measurement date. The text also does not say where the 720-880 m distances are measured from. The pack compares eastbound and westbound data elsewhere, and ASK-4 itself says 'Eastbound'. So the claim should state the direction and date, and cite FOI-1730-1819#001, which holds that information. The response's 'noise' was measured at nearby homes, so 'likely cause of the noise' should not be read as in-train noise.
source_evidence: FOI-1730-1819#001 (attachment 'Rail Roughness Plots BEG-MIE January 2018'): 'Central line Rail Roughness Plots / Eastbound Bethnal Green to Mile End / Figure 1 – LHR 30-100mm ...'. FOI-1730-1819#000: 'The rail roughness measurements confirm an elevated rail roughness levels between 720 and 880m which are the likely cause of the noise at this site.' and 'the noise measurements in the below tables are from residential properties in the vicinity'.
suggested_wording: TfL said its rail roughness measurements 'confirm an elevated rail roughness levels between 720 and 880m'. The attached plots, dated January 2018, cover the eastbound track from Bethnal Green to Mile End (cite FOI-1730-1819#001).

phrase: the continuous rail grinding programme is confirmed around eight weeks in advance of works
problem: This falls under 'TfL states', but the cited source is the Mayor's written answer to MQ 2022/2799 (20 December 2022, to Caroline Pidgeon AM), not a TfL document. The Mayor is describing TfL's practice. An Assembly Member will tell a Mayor's answer apart from a TfL statement. The claim also cuts the end of the sentence and the next sentence, which say grinding for noise comes last: safety and operationally critical work is prioritised, and noise and vibration grinding is planned only once defect grinding is scheduled and spare capacity found. Placed next to 'must be repeated ... (usually 6 months to a year)', the cut makes noise grinding sound like a regular cycle. The source says it fills spare capacity. Both statements are from December 2022, which the present tense 'states' hides, although MQT 2026/2156 shows TfL still gives the eight-week answer.
source_evidence: MQ-2022-2799#000 ('Asked of: | The Mayor'; Answer dated 'Tuesday 20 December 2022'): 'TfL's continuous rail grinding programme is confirmed around eight weeks in advance of works, with safety and operationally critical work prioritised. Once grinding to address defects has been scheduled and spare capacity identified, grinding to address noise and vibration can be planned.'
suggested_wording: ...and the Mayor's answer to MQ 2022/2799 (20 December 2022) says 'TfL's continuous rail grinding programme is confirmed around eight weeks in advance of works, with safety and operationally critical work prioritised'. It adds that grinding for noise and vibration is planned only once grinding for defects has been scheduled and spare capacity identified.

phrase: whereas in FOI-2986-2324 (published 12 December 2023) TfL stated that it did not have a study on in-carriage Tube noise at the moment
problem: The quote is taken out of context. The 'no study' sentence answers the requester's question 6 about research opportunities. It is not a statement about whether TfL measures or works on in-carriage noise. 'Whereas' sets it against the bi-monthly readings as if TfL contradicted itself, but routine readings and a research study are different things. The same 2023 response released cab levels and said rail grinding is TfL's primary way of addressing in-carriage levels. A reader (or TfL, in reply) could fairly say the pack implies TfL said it held no in-carriage noise data or work, and the source contradicts that. The two FOIs are also eight months apart, and only one is dated in the claim: FOI-1231-2425 was published 08 August 2024, after the 'no study' reply. Minor point folded in here: TfL released a table of levels, not audio 'recordings' (the PDF is only titled 'Central Line cab recordings').
source_evidence: FOI-2986-2324#000: "Are there any research opportunities for me to join or further investigate? We don't have anyone trying to research this topic, so I am not sure, but I wonder if Anthony and Chris feel this is something they could support from an engineering perspective?\nWe don't have a study on in-carriage Tube noise on the London Underground at the moment. I have passed your email onto my colleagues who deal with this issue for their attention." Same chunk, answer to Q5: "However, rail grinding is our primary method of addressing in-carriage levels." Also: "The attached table, which contains data taken on 4 September 2023, provides the levels and 1/3rd octaves in a Central line train cab..." FOI-1231-2425#000: "Date published: 08 August 2024".
suggested_wording: Split C07 into two claims and drop 'whereas'. Claim A: "In FOI-2986-2324 (published 12 December 2023), TfL released a table of levels measured in a Central line train cab on 4 September 2023 for the entire tunnel sections between White City and Newbury Park: 89 dB Leq A eastbound and 83 dB Leq A westbound. Answering a question about research opportunities, the same response said: 'We don't have a study on in-carriage Tube noise on the London Underground at the moment.'" Claim B: the bi-monthly statement, worded as in the next finding.

phrase: TfL stated that in-cab noise readings on the Central line are carried out on a bi-monthly period
problem: TfL did not say the routine readings are in-cab. The requester asked how often readings are carried out on 'this line', and TfL answered 'Readings are carried out on a bi-monthly period.' The cab location is stated only for the 24 June 2024 figures. So 'in-cab' is the agent's inference, and ASK 3 builds on it ('Disclose all bi-monthly in-cab noise measurements'). 'Bi-monthly' is also ambiguous (every two months or twice a month), so TfL's exact words should stay in quotation marks.
source_evidence: FOI-1231-2425#000: "And also how often readings are carried out on this line?\nReadings are carried out on a bi-monthly period." Separately, for the disclosed figures only: "these measurements were taken from within the train operator's cab."
suggested_wording: "In FOI-1231-2425 (published 08 August 2024), asked how often noise readings are carried out on the Central line, TfL replied: 'Readings are carried out on a bi-monthly period.' The 24 June 2024 figures in that response were taken from within the train operator's cab."

phrase: yielding a pre-registered NO-GO verdict because the difference is below 1 dB and within limiter compression and run-to-run variation
problem: The claim gives the wrong reason for the verdict, an unsupported causal link. Under the frozen rule, NO-GO is returned only when LST-BTH is not higher on every placement-ok trip. A difference under 1 dB with every trip positive gives WEAK, not NO-GO. 23 Oct alone shows this: +0.60 dB, positive on 5/5 trips, verdict WEAK. The verdict became NO-GO because one of the 11 trips (R10, westbound, -0.13 dB) went the other way. The claim also leaves out the stat's other stated limit, that the level variants do not agree in every trip. A reader would take it that the direction was confirmed and only the size was too small to resolve, which is not what the pre-registered test found. Note: the pack's fixed Method text in agent/pack.py says the same thing ('the difference was under 1 dB, inside the phone's limiter compression (a pre-registered NO-GO)'), so it needs the same fix to stay consistent.
source_evidence: scripts/loudness.py verdict(), identical at git tag prereg-24oct: consistent = la["n_positive"] == n; "if consistent and la["mean_db"] >= MIN_DB and all(robust.values()): v = "GO" / elif consistent: v = "WEAK" / else: v = "NO-GO"". Stat loudness.verdict justification: "LST-BTH is louder than BTH-MLE in 10/11 placement-ok trips ... Not robust across variants: LAeq, nospeech_LAeq, core_LAeq, LAeq_1s_mean, LAeq_limiter_ub do not agree in every trip." outputs/FINDINGS.md: "The frozen rule now says NO-GO; on 23 Oct alone it said WEAK." Also, for 23 Oct: "+0.60 dB. It is positive on 5/5 trips". outputs/gonogo/loudness.json per_trip R10_WB_MLE-LST: diff_LAeq -0.133.
suggested_wording: "..., so the pre-registered check returned NO-GO: the rule needs the Liverpool Street-Bethnal Green section to be higher on every trip, and one westbound trip went the other way. The difference is also below 1 dB, which is inside the Voice Memos limiter compression and the run-to-run variation, and the level variants do not all agree."

phrase: than the quietest measured sub-surface section, eastbound Aldgate East to Whitechapel (-25.52 dBFS(A))
problem: The claim leaves out what a reader needs to judge this comparison, and the pack shows only stat keys, so the reader cannot find it anywhere else. (1) The comparison section is on the Hammersmith & City line (rides R13 and R15), a different line with different trains. The project's own FINDINGS treat cross-line level comparisons as confounded ('Different line and rolling stock'). So the gap cannot say anything specific about the Liverpool Street-Bethnal Green section, which is the pack's question. (2) The comparison mean rests on only 2 runs (-26.85 and -24.18; sd 1.89 dB, about five times the LST-BTH sd of 0.35). One of them (R15) is a partial section: its arrival at Whitechapel was not recorded, segment confidence 0.4. C08 gives n and sd; C10 gives neither. (3) It is the lowest of four noisy H&C means, which pushes the gap up. Against the other three, the gap would be about 4.0 to 6.0 dB, and against the two individual ALE-WCL runs it is 5.5 to 8.2 dB, so the two-decimal '6.86' suggests precision the data do not have. (4) The limiter was engaged on 37-48 % of LST-BTH seconds but only 11-24 % of ALE-WCL seconds, so this relative gap is not a dB(A) difference.
source_evidence: Stat level.EB.ALE-WCL: value -25.52, n 2, detail.sd 1.89, runs "R13,R15". Stat level.EB.LST-BTH: n 6, sd 0.35. Other sub-surface stats: level.EB.LST-ALE -22.67 (n 2, sd 2.42); level.WB.WCL-ALE -24.54 (n 1); level.WB.ALE-LST -24.65 (n 1). outputs/FINDINGS.md: "Hammersmith & City LST⇄WCL: R13 and R15 eastbound, R14 westbound." Also, on cross-line comparison: "Different line and rolling stock, one run, and the absolute levels are uncalibrated." outputs/qc.json R15_EB_LST-WCL: "section_truncated ... ALE->WCL: arrive not recorded". outputs/gonogo/loudness_sections.csv: ALE->WCL LAeq R13 -26.849, R15 -24.181 (seg_confidence 0.4). limited_frac: LST->BTH runs 0.37-0.48; ALE->WCL runs 0.109 and 0.241.
suggested_wording: "In our uncalibrated relative phone-audio measurements, eastbound Liverpool Street to Bethnal Green on the Central line (-18.66 dBFS(A), n=6, sd=0.35) was 6.86 dB higher in relative level than the quietest section we recorded on the Hammersmith & City line, a sub-surface line with different trains: eastbound Aldgate East to Whitechapel (-25.52 dBFS(A), n=2, sd=1.89). The two sections are on different lines and trains, so this gap shows nothing specific about the Liverpool Street-Bethnal Green track, and it is not a calibrated dB(A) difference."

phrase: and the eight weeks forward grinding programme
problem: The claim says the Mayor committed to ensuring TfL provides the eight-week forward grinding programme. He did not commit to that. He said he could 'not see a reason why' it cannot be provided, and that he would take the matter away and write to the Assembly. The claim's own cited quote ('I cannot see a reason why the eight weeks programme cannot be provided') is an opinion, used here as if it were a commitment. The items the Mayor said he would 'make sure' TfL provides were the six-month grinding information, track renewal programmes and alternative noise measures. The eight-week programme came up only afterwards, when Ms Baker said TfL had refused a six-month plan and had not offered the eight weeks. This misstates who committed to what. The commitment was also about the information TfL gives at its regular meetings with Assembly Members, which the claim leaves out.
source_evidence: MQT-2026-2156#003 (Mayor): "I will write to the Assembly, if that is OK, because I suspect it is an issue for all Members of the Assembly in relation to a forward programme of meetings with the Assembly, what additional information will be provided, and I cannot see a reason why the eight weeks programme cannot be provided. I take the point about when you get the tracks and stuff, but, Chair, let me take this away with your permission and come back to all the Assembly." Same chunk (Baker): "the response I have says, 'We cannot do that because it is only planned eight weeks in advance'. Fine. Did it offer to tell us eight weeks in advance? No, it just did not answer that at all." Firm wording is used only for the other items, MQT-2026-2156#002: "TfL meets every few months with Members of the Assembly. What I will do is ensure that the information it provides is far, far, far more detailed than is currently received ... I will make sure it provides, in addition, information on what in real-time rail grinding activity is taking place over the next six months, the track renewal programmes, alternative noise reduction measures".
suggested_wording: At Mayor's Question Time on 16 July 2026 (Question 2026/2156), Elly Baker AM said TfL's Government Relations had sent an email turning down the majority of her data requests. The Mayor said he would ensure the information TfL provides at its regular meetings with Assembly Members is 'far, far, far more detailed', including information on rail grinding over the next six months, track renewal programmes and alternative noise reduction measures. On the eight-week grinding programme, which Ms Baker said TfL had not offered, the Mayor said he could 'not see a reason why the eight weeks programme cannot be provided' and that he would take the matter away and write to the Assembly.

phrase: Publicly available TfL documents do not specify
problem: This is an unhedged statement about everything TfL has published, but the agent reviewed a fixed corpus of 14 documents (44 chunks). Only two of them are TfL's six-monthly updates to the Assembly (Aug 2024, Aug 2025). The corpus itself refers to TfL publications that were not reviewed: the February update letters, the data packs attached to both updates, and a twice-yearly series of updates running since Dec 2022. Finding nothing in 14 documents does not show that TfL has published nothing. The claim is typed 'inference', which must be hedged, and it is a Summary headline, so an over-broad negative here could be refuted by a single TfL letter. Within the corpus the content holds. MQ 2022/1791 and its original attachment.xlsx give section names only, with no track or chainage. Neither update names LST-BTH or BTH-MLE. The 2024 update counts deep Tube reconditioning sites without naming them.
source_evidence: TfL-noise-update-2024-08#000: "As referenced in my previous letter in February, updates cover spans of six calendar months, from January to June, and from July to December"; TfL-noise-update-2025-08#001: "I mentioned in February that we were exploring the use of variable speeds"; TfL-noise-update-2024-08#003: "The related data pack on noise and vibration complaints received between January and June 2024 is attached."; TfL-noise-update-2025-08#003: "Please find attached a corresponding data pack conveying noise and vibration monitoring over the past six months."; Weir-letter-2022-12#000: "We are committed to providing the Assembly with twice-yearly written updates on our work to tackle Tube noise across the network." None of these February letters or data packs is in the corpus (doc list: 14 docs, the only TfL updates are 2024-08 and 2025-08). Supporting the within-corpus content: MQ-2022-1791#001 lists only "Bethnal Green to Liverpool Street" / "Mile End to Bethnal Green"; TfL-noise-update-2024-08#000: "We have completed PV conversion to Delkor as part of Deep Tube Reconditioning at seven locations" (sites not named).
suggested_wording: In the documents we reviewed, we found no statement of which track (eastbound, westbound or both) or which chainages were ground on these two sections in the grinding window reported in the Mayor's written answer (C01), which lists them only as 'Bethnal Green to Liverpool Street' and 'Mile End to Bethnal Green'. We also found no record of grinding on either section since then, and no confirmation that the planned Eastbound Liverpool Street to Bethnal Green deep Tube reconditioning was completed. We did not review all of TfL's six-monthly updates to the Assembly or their data packs, so TfL may hold or may already have published this information. (No numerals are used, because inference claims may not add numbers.)

phrase: her requests for Tube noise data
problem: Ms Baker made the requests in a letter to TfL Commissioner Andy Lord. By her own account they were for data on residents' noise and vibration casework, complaints and the measures taken, and she said her focus was residential noise. The pack is about in-carriage noise on two sections, so 'Tube noise data' could suggest she was refused section-level in-train noise measurements. The transcript does not say that.
source_evidence: MQT-2026-2156#001: "It is the residential noise and vibration that I want to focus on ... last month I wrote to Andy Lord [Commissioner of TfL] direct. In that letter I asked for a significant improvement in the quality and quantity of data. I asked for specific data based on the residents' casework that we dealt with ... to monitor the issue, look at the measures being taken and specifics on complaints. Last week, I received an email, not from Andy Lord ... just an email from TfL's Government Relations turning down the majority of the requests for data."
suggested_wording: her data requests (made in a letter to TfL Commissioner Andy Lord, for data on residents' noise and vibration casework, complaints and the measures being taken)

phrase: because the built-in microphone is validated only up to a limited level, these readings are indicative, may read low
problem: The caveat leaves out two limits that the cited stats and FINDINGS.md state. (1) The validated limit is about 85 dB(A), and both readings are above it; saying 'a limited level' hides why they may read low. (2) There was one trip per direction, on different trains. C11 is a Summary headline shown directly after TfL's EB/WB figures (C05), and it sets EB 91.9 beside WB 87.3. A reader may take the 4.6 dB gap as a direction or track effect. The project's own analysis says the data cannot separate train from direction, and same-evening Voice Memos rides showed the opposite sign. The fixed method note gives the ~85 dB(A) limit but not 'different trains'.
source_evidence: section_stats niosh.EB.LST-MLE / niosh.WB.MLE-LST detail.limits: "iPhone built-in mic validated to ~0.5 dB(A) only up to ~85 dB (Huyan et al. 2023); these trips are above that, so readings may be low; not a certified meter: indicative; n = 1 trip per direction; different trains". outputs/FINDINGS.md post-hoc 1: "Eastbound minus westbound trip level is +4.6 dB on NIOSH but −0.5 dB on Voice Memos (same-evening rides)" and "One NIOSH trip per direction, on different trains, cannot separate a train effect from a direction effect." data/raw/niosh.csv notes: N1 "2nd car, car [number redacted]", N2 "2nd car, car [number redacted]".
suggested_wording: ...because the app on the iPhone's built-in microphone is validated only up to about 85 dB(A), below both readings, these readings are indicative and may read low. Each direction is a single trip on a different train, so the eastbound-westbound difference may reflect the train rather than the direction or track. The readings are not like-for-like with TfL's per-section in-cab figures.

phrase: the underlying TfL dataset, date, and measurement location (cab versus saloon) for that 92.8 figure are not in the primary corpus
problem: 'The underlying TfL dataset' states in the pack's own voice that a TfL dataset lies behind 92.8. Only the secondary article says that ('According to the TfL data'). No primary document reviewed contains the figure: TfL's own disclosed in-cab figure for this section is 87 dB LAeq eastbound and 86 westbound. The article also gives no frequency weighting, only 'decibels' and 'average noise levels'. 'Primary corpus' is internal jargon a reader may not follow. The conclusion is right, but the phrase slightly undercuts the rule that 92.8 is a press report, not TfL data.
source_evidence: BrixtonBuzz-2026-01-27#000: "According to the TfL data, the highest recorded average noise levels in the dataset were found on the following station-to-station sections: ... Liverpool Street to Bethnal Green (Central line) – 92.8 decibels" and "[ Thanks to JRPass for the information ]". A search of all 44 chunks finds 92.8 only in this chunk. FOI-1231-2425#000: "Liverpool Street to Bethnal Green | 87" (EB) and "Bethnal Green to Liverpool Street | 86" (WB), in-cab, 24 June 2024.
suggested_wording: A secondary press article in Brixton Buzz (27 January 2026) reported 92.8 decibels for Liverpool Street to Bethnal Green, describing it as 'TfL data' and thanking JRPass 'for the information'. We found no source for this figure in the primary documents we reviewed, and the article does not give the measurement date, frequency weighting or position (cab or saloon). It is a press report and cannot be treated as TfL's own data.

phrase: during that earlier grinding window
problem: This refers back to a window that only C01 defines (Dec 2021-May 2022, MQ 2022/1791). The pack shows C15 last in the Summary, after C09, and again in section 4 after C14 (the 92.8 claim). In neither place does 'that earlier grinding window' have a nearby antecedent. A reader could link it to the February 2019 grinding in C02 instead.
source_evidence: agent/pack.py renders headline_claim_ids in order [C01, C05, C11, C09, C15], then the 'limits' section as C14, C15. MQ-2022-1791#001: "Sections of the London Underground that have benefited from rail grinding to help reduce noise levels (December 2021-May 2022)". FOI-1730-1819#000 (another grinding window, cited in C02): "We will undertake rail grinding at this location in February 2019".
suggested_wording: during the grinding window reported in the Mayor's written answer cited in C01. An inference claim may not add numbers, so to name the dates, change this clause to a sourced claim citing MQ-2022-1791#001: "between December 2021 and May 2022 (Mayor's Question 2022/1791)".

phrase: the Mayor committed to ensuring TfL provides far more detailed information, including real-time rail grinding activity over the next six months, track renewal programmes, and the eight weeks forward grinding programme
problem: This overstates what the Mayor committed to. He did promise that TfL's information to Members would be 'far, far, far more detailed', including grinding activity over the next six months and track renewal programmes. On the eight-week programme, though, he only said he could not see why it could not be provided, then said he would 'take this away' and write to the Assembly. That is not a commitment to provide it. The claim also leaves out that Baker said TfL had refused her request for a six-month forward plan because grinding is 'only planned eight weeks in advance'; that is the tension with C04's eight-week planning, and the pack never reconciles the two. Finally, the claim does not say that Baker described her refused data requests as based on residents' casework (residential noise and vibration), not in-train section data.
source_evidence: MQT-2026-2156#002 (Mayor): 'What I will do is ensure that the information it provides is far, far, far more detailed than is currently received... I will make sure it provides, in addition, information on what in real-time rail grinding activity is taking place over the next six months, the track renewal programmes...'; MQT-2026-2156#003 (Mayor): 'I will write to the Assembly ... and I cannot see a reason why the eight weeks programme cannot be provided. I take the point about when you get the tracks and stuff, but, Chair, let me take this away with your permission and come back to all the Assembly.'; MQT-2026-2156#003 (Baker): 'you have mentioned a forward plan of rail grinding for six months that I asked, the response I have says, "We cannot do that because it is only planned eight weeks in advance"'; MQT-2026-2156#001 (Baker): 'It is the residential noise and vibration that I want to focus on' and 'I asked for specific data based on the residents' casework that we dealt with.'
suggested_wording: ...and the Mayor said he would make sure the information TfL gives Members is 'far, far, far more detailed', including rail grinding activity over the next six months and track renewal programmes. Baker said TfL had declined her request for a six-month forward plan because grinding 'is only planned eight weeks in advance'. On that eight-week programme the Mayor said 'I cannot see a reason why the eight weeks programme cannot be provided' and undertook to 'take this away' and write to the Assembly.

phrase: headline_claim_ids ["C01", "C05", "C11", "C09", "C15"]
problem: On balance the Summary is fair. It shows the pre-registered NO-GO (C09), labels the app readings indicative, and rests on TfL's own cab data. What it never says is that the evidence contains no TfL in-train measurement of either section from before the Dec 2021 to May 2022 grinding. Read in order (ground for noise, then 87/86 dB two years later), together with C04 ('repeated ... usually 6 months to a year') and ASK-1 ('to know if maintenance has lapsed'), it invites the 'grinding wore off / noise returned' reading that the pack must not make. TfL could answer that levels are lower than before grinding, or that it has re-ground since.
source_evidence: The only in-train figures in the corpus are post-grinding: FOI-1231-2425#000 'noise levels recorded on the Monday 24 June 2024'; FOI-2986-2324#000 'data taken on 4 September 2023 ... for the entire tunnel sections between White City and Newbury Park'. The 2018 FOI figures are residential: FOI-1730-1819#000 'the noise measurements in the below tables are from residential properties in the vicinity of the location in question'.
suggested_wording: Add a hedged limits claim (no numbers) and include it in the Summary: 'The documents we reviewed contain no TfL in-train noise measurement for either section from before that grinding window, so they cannot show whether the grinding lowered noise or whether levels have risen since.'

phrase: states that it uses a data-led approach analysing network-wide corrugation data to prioritise grinding (C13)
problem: Wrong cross-reference. C13's text (Baker's refused data requests and the Mayor's transparency commitments) says nothing about a data-led approach. The only related words in C13's sources are Baker calling 'the data-led approach' a 'catch-all phrase'. The network-wide description is accurate, but it comes from TfL's August 2025 update, which no verified claim cites. So this sentence reaches the AM without passing the verifier, and anyone who checks C13 will not find it.
source_evidence: TfL-noise-update-2025-08#000: 'we employ a data-led approach to tackle its growth. This approach analyses data from the entire network to determine where rail defects occur and establish where corrugation has worsened, allowing us to tailor and prioritise rail grinding schedules'. C13 cites only MQT-2026-2156#001-#003. MQT-2026-2156#001 (Baker): 'that catch-all phrase ... the data-led approach. If there is all this data, I do not quite know why they cannot just share it with us.'
suggested_wording: Why: TfL previously disclosed January 2018 rail roughness plots for eastbound Bethnal Green to Mile End under FOI-1730-1819 (C02). Its August 2025 update says its data-led approach 'analyses data from the entire network to determine where rail defects occur and establish where corrugation has worsened' to prioritise grinding (add this as a verified sourced claim and cite it here instead of C13). As Elly Baker AM put it at Mayor's Question Time, if that data exists it can be shared. Current roughness data would show whether rail roughness on these sections is elevated now.

phrase: because grinding must be repeated every six to twelve months to maintain effectiveness (C04), post-May 2022 logs are required to know if maintenance has lapsed
problem: This hardens TfL's 'usually 6 months - a year' into a fixed 'every six to twelve months', then frames the request as checking whether 'maintenance has lapsed', as if every site had a due date. TfL's stated process is that noise grinding is planned once defect grinding has been scheduled and spare capacity found, and is prioritised by data, so TfL can simply reply that no re-grind was due. The 'lapsed' framing also feeds the implied 'noise returned' reading (see the PACK Summary finding).
source_evidence: CSOPP-2022-12-tube-noise#001: 'It must be repeated at regular intervals ... (usually 6 months [-] a year), to maintain effectiveness'. MQ-2022-2799#000: 'TfL's continuous rail grinding programme is confirmed around eight weeks in advance of works, with safety and operationally critical work prioritised. Once grinding to address defects has been scheduled and spare capacity identified, grinding to address noise and vibration can be planned.'
suggested_wording: Why: Mayor's Question 2022/1791 lists both sections as ground for noise between December 2021 and May 2022 without stating track direction or chainage (C01). TfL says grinding must be repeated at regular intervals, usually every 6 months to a year, to stay effective (C04), and that noise grinding is planned once defect grinding is scheduled and spare capacity is found. The record since May 2022 shows whether these sections have been re-ground.

phrase: subsequent Assembly updates do not state whether this site was among those completed or still in progress (C15)
problem: The corpus holds only two later updates, August 2024 and August 2025. Earlier updates and TfL's February updates exist and were not reviewed, so 'subsequent Assembly updates do not state' overreaches in the same way as C15. The two updates that were reviewed give counts without site names, and the 2025 one does not mention the Central line at all. That is worth saying precisely.
source_evidence: TfL-noise-update-2024-08#000: 'We have completed PV conversion to Delkor as part of Deep Tube Reconditioning at seven locations' / 'Nine sites are in the process of Deep Tube Reconditioning, with a further three planned to begin this financial year' (no site names), and 'As referenced in my previous letter in February'. TfL-noise-update-2025-08#000-#003 contain no mention of the Central line, Liverpool Street, Bethnal Green or Mile End.
suggested_wording: Why: TfL's December 2022 letter listed Liverpool Street to Bethnal Green Eastbound for deep Tube reconditioning in 2023/24 (C03). TfL's August 2024 update reports conversions completed at seven locations and nine sites in progress without naming them, and its August 2025 update does not mention this site. We have not reviewed TfL's other six-monthly updates.

phrase: while our indicative saloon app readings and secondary reports suggest high levels (C11, C14)
problem: This uses the secondary 92.8 dB report as support for 'high levels', although C14 says the figure 'cannot be treated as primary TfL data'. The request also assumes the figure 'was drawn' from a TfL disclosure or dataset. Its origin is unknown, and TfL cannot say what JRPass used. Asking whether any TfL dataset contains the figure avoids assuming the answer.
source_evidence: BrixtonBuzz-2026-01-27#000: 'According to the TfL data, the highest recorded average noise levels in the dataset were found on the following station-to-station sections' ... 'Liverpool Street to Bethnal Green (Central line) - 92.8 decibels' ... 'Thanks to JRPass for the information'. C14: 'so it cannot be treated as primary TfL data'.
suggested_wording: Request: '...and say whether any TfL disclosure or dataset contains the 92.8 dB figure for Liverpool Street to Bethnal Green that Brixton Buzz, crediting JRPass, attributed to "TfL data".' Why: '...our indicative whole-trip app readings were also high (C11). A press report attributes a 92.8 dB figure to TfL data, but its source, date and measurement position are unknown (C14).'

phrase: was 6.86 dB higher in relative level than the quietest measured sub-surface section, eastbound Aldgate East to Whitechapel (-25.52 dBFS(A))
problem: The comparator is the most extreme one available: a different line (Hammersmith & City), different trains and a different tunnel type, with n=2 and sd 1.89, compared across rides. The project's own plots call cross-run comparisons of these uncalibrated levels weak. A reader may take it to mean 'LST-BTH is about 7 dB louder than normal', and it says nothing about grinding.
source_evidence: section_stats level.EB.ALE-WCL: value -25.52, n 2, sd 1.89, runs 'R13,R15' (H&C rides). scripts/loudness.py axis label: 'section LAeq, dB(A) re full scale (uncalibrated; cross-run comparisons are weak)'.
suggested_wording: In our uncalibrated relative phone audio, eastbound Liverpool Street to Bethnal Green (-18.66 dBFS(A)) was 6.86 dB higher than eastbound Aldgate East to Whitechapel on the Hammersmith & City line (-25.52 dBFS(A), n=2, sd=1.89), the quietest section we recorded. This compares different lines, trains and tunnel types across rides, which our method treats as a weak comparison.
